artiest/maria-schneider.text:
Maria Schneider was born in 1960 in Windom, Minnesota. She studied composition at the University of Minnesota and the Eastman School of Music. She then became a copyist and assistant to Gil Evans, with whom she worked on music for a tour with Sting and on the film score of The Color of Money. She also studied with Bob Brookmeyer. In 1992 she founded the Maria Schneider Jazz Orchestra, which from 1993 played every week at Visiones in Greenwich Village. Their first album, Evanescence, was released in 1994.

Her orchestra has won several Grammys. Concert in the Garden (2004) was the first album to win, and the first to be made through ArtistShare, a platform on which fans fund the production. The Thompson Fields and Data Lords followed, and Schneider herself received Grammys for individual pieces on Sky Blue and Data Lords. On Winter Morning Walks (2013) she works with the soprano Dawn Upshaw, chamber orchestras and poems by Ted Kooser.

Schneider writes for a large jazz band, but her work sounds more like orchestral music with improvisation than like a traditional big band. She is also an outspoken advocate for the rights of musicians and speaks out against streaming models and big data companies, which she also worked into titles such as Data Lords. This makes her one of the best-known voices of the contemporary big band.
artiest/maria-schneider.listen: Listen to Cerulean Skies and notice how the orchestra sounds like one great palette. Can you hear how the soloist rises above the broadly worked-out accompaniment, as if you were looking at a landscape?

artiest/maria-severa.text:
Maria Severa Onofriana, known simply as A Severa, was a Portuguese fado singer and guitarist. She was born in 1820 in the Madragoa district of Lisbon and died in 1846, only twenty-six years old. Her father was of Roma descent, and her mother, who came from Ovar, ran a tavern. Severa is said to have sung fado in those taverns, accompanying herself on the Portuguese guitar. She is described as a tall, charming courtesan. One of her lovers was the Count of Vimioso. She died of tuberculosis in Lisbon and was buried in a common grave.

Fado, which roughly means fate, is sometimes called the Portuguese blues. It is a song full of longing and wistfulness, accompanied by guitars. Severa is regarded as the first fado singer to become famous, and after her death she acquired an almost mythical status. Her fame grew partly thanks to the novel A Severa by Júlio Dantas, which became a play in 1901. In 1931 the director Leitão de Barros made the first Portuguese sound film of it, also called A Severa. In 2011 a romantic musical about her premiered in Canada.

Maria Severa shows how fado arose in the poorest neighbourhoods of Lisbon. Singers such as Amália Rodrigues later built on this tradition.
artiest/maria-severa.listen: Listen to a fado and notice the Portuguese guitar with its bright, trembling strings and the voice that almost tells the song. Can you hear how the word saudade, longing, resonates in the melody?

artiest/mariachi-vargas-de-tecalitlan.text:
Mariachi Vargas de Tecalitlán is a Mexican mariachi ensemble founded in 1896 in Tecalitlán, in southern Jalisco, by Gaspar Vargas. In the beginning they played with a guitarra de golpe, a wooden harp and two violins: the Sonido Tecalitlán, which differed from the Sonido Cocula of the neighbouring village. His son Silvestre took over in 1931, expanded the group and dreamed that it would become the best mariachi in Mexico. The musicians wore charro suits, arrived on time and did not drink, which stood out in those years.

In 1933 they won a competition in Guadalajara, and in 1934 one in Mexico City. President Lázaro Cárdenas, a fan of the group, had them appointed as the official mariachi of the Mexico City police, where they kept playing in parks and gardens for twenty years. From 1937 they appeared in films, the first of more than two hundred, including those of Pedro Infante. That same year they made their first record. In 1941 the group adopted the trumpet for good, with Miguel Martínez Domínguez as its first trumpeter. In 1944 Rubén Fuentes, a classically trained violinist, joined and became the arranger. Together with Silvestre he renewed the sound and the professional image of the mariachi. From 1950 the ensemble was under his artistic direction. Records such as El Mejor Mariachi del Mundo (1958) and La voz de México (1962) represent this period.

A standard mariachi has violins, trumpets, guitarrón, guitar and vihuela. The ensemble is regarded as the standard against which other mariachis are measured. In this way the music grew from village festival to a symbol of Mexico.
artiest/mariachi-vargas-de-tecalitlan.listen: Listen to La Negra and notice the trumpets taking up the melody together with the violins. Can you hear how the rhythm of the guitarrón and vihuela beneath them determines the movement?

artiest/mariinsky-orchestra.text:
The Mariinsky Orchestra is the orchestra of the Mariinsky Theatre in Saint Petersburg, alongside the Mariinsky Ballet and the Mariinsky Opera. The theatre opened in 1860 and in the late nineteenth century became the most important musical theatre in Russia. Many stage works by Tchaikovsky, Mussorgsky and Rimsky-Korsakov had their premiere there. The name refers to Empress Maria Alexandrovna, the wife of Tsar Alexander II.

The name of the building changed with the political times. It was the Imperial Mariinsky Theatre until 1920, then a state theatre and, from 1935 to 1992, the Kirov Theatre, named after the assassinated party leader Sergei Kirov. Since 1992 it has been called the Mariinsky again. The companies kept the name Kirov for the sake of their reputation abroad. After the departure of Yuri Temirkanov in 1988, the conductor Valery Gergiev became general director of the theatre.

The orchestra thus plays the Russian repertoire for which the theatre is known, from opera and ballet to symphonic music. Our sources say little about its recordings and its line-up. For pop history it matters mainly as the place where the great Russian repertoire of the nineteenth century was performed.
artiest/mariinsky-orchestra.listen: Listen to an excerpt from a Tchaikovsky ballet played by the Mariinsky Orchestra and notice the full strings and the way the melody is passed between the sections of the orchestra.

artiest/marika-ninou.text:
Marika Ninou was an Armenian-Greek singer of rebetiko. She was born in 1922 on board the ship Evangelistria, which was carrying her mother, two sisters and eight-year-old brother from Smyrna to Piraeus. Because it was thought she would not survive, she was laid in a storeroom after the birth. She pulled through, and the captain immediately christened her Evangelia. The family settled in Kokkinia, a poor district near Piraeus. At school she learned to play the mandolin, and she sang in the Armenian church.

She married in 1939. In 1947 her husband left for Armenia, leaving her with her son. She performed with the acrobat Nikos Nikolaides in the duo Nino. In 1948 she recorded two songs with Manolis Chiotis. From 1949 she worked with Vassilis Tsitsanis at the club Fat Jimmy's. The duo of Tsitsanis and Ninou became important for Greek music. In 1951 they performed together in Istanbul, after which they went their separate ways. In 1954 she went to the United States for a cancer operation. The disease spread quickly and she returned to Greece, where she kept singing for a little while in great pain. She died in 1957, thirty-five years old.

Ninou had a high, powerful voice. Rebetiko, the urban folk song of Piraeus and Athens, acquired a feminine, melancholy face through her. Her voice is the best known from the collaboration with Tsitsanis.
artiest/marika-ninou.listen: Listen to a song by Marika Ninou with Tsitsanis and notice her high, clear voice and the bouzouki carrying the melody along. Try to hear how the song laments without becoming heavy.

artiest/marillion.text:
Marillion is a British neo-prog band, formed in 1979 in Aylesbury, Buckinghamshire. The group emerged from British post-punk and formed a bridge between punk rock and classic progressive rock. It became the commercially most successful neo-prog band of the 1980s. The first single, Market Square Heroes, was released in 1982, and a year later came the first album, Script for a Jester's Tear. In total the band made twenty studio albums.

Between 1983 and 1994 Marillion had eight albums in the British top ten. Misplaced Childhood from 1985 reached number one and produced the singles Kayleigh and Lavender. Kayleigh reached the American Hot 100. Clutching at Straws from 1987 was the last album with the original singer Fish, who went solo at the end of 1988. In 1989 Steve Hogarth became the singer, with Seasons End as the first album. The band left EMI in 1996 and in the years that followed grew into a cult group with a loyal worldwide following.

Marillion is regarded as a pioneer of crowdfunding and fan-funded music. The sound revolves around long songs with keyboards, melodic guitar and a singer who tells stories, in a theatrical tone. Misplaced Childhood is a concept album. In School of Rock, Garden Party from 1983 and Kayleigh from 1985 belong to that wave of prog rock in the 1980s, when old forms were used anew.
artiest/marillion.listen: Listen to Kayleigh by Marillion. Notice the keyboards and the guitar accompanying the love story, and how the singer narrates rather than shouts.

artiest/marin-alsop.text:
Marin Alsop is an American conductor, born in 1956 in New York to two professional musicians who played string instruments. She grew up in Manhattan, studied violin at the Juilliard School and played in orchestras such as the New York Philharmonic. She was turned down three times for Juilliard's conducting programme. So in 1981 she founded the New York String Ensemble, then the all-female jazz ensemble String Fever and, in 1984, Concordia, an orchestra of fifty musicians for twentieth-century American music.

In 1983 she played first violin on the recording of The Photographer by Philip Glass, and in 1985 on the original cast recording of the musical Big River. In 1989 she became the first woman to win the Koussevitzky Prize at the Tanglewood Music Center, where she met her hero and mentor Leonard Bernstein. In 2005 she received a MacArthur Fellowship, the Genius Grant. She led the Cabrillo Festival of Contemporary Music from 1992 to 2016 and the Colorado Symphony from 1993 to 2005. She became music director of the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra and is now chief conductor of the Polish National Radio Symphony Orchestra. Her recordings include Victory Stride, on the symphonic music of James P. Johnson, from 1994, and Fanfares for the Uncommon Woman from 1999.

Alsop showed that women can stand at the head of the greatest orchestras. She combines classical, contemporary and American music, including that of jazz composers.
artiest/marin-alsop.listen: Listen to Victory Stride, the symphonic music of James P. Johnson played by Alsop, and notice how jazz rhythms and piano style are worked into an orchestral piece.

artiest/mario-bauza.text:
Mario Bauzá was a Cuban trumpeter, saxophonist, arranger and bandleader. He was born in Havana in 1911 and was a child prodigy on the clarinet; at the age of eleven he was already playing with the Havana symphony orchestra. In 1926 he came to New York with a Cuban orchestra. The jazz in Harlem made such an impression that he returned in 1930. He learned to play the trumpet in two weeks in order to be able to step in on a recording session, and Louis Armstrong became his model. From 1933 he was first trumpeter and musical director of Chick Webb's orchestra, where he met Dizzy Gillespie. He then played with Cab Calloway and made sure that Gillespie was hired there too.

In 1939 he founded the band Machito and his Afro-Cubans with his brother-in-law, the singer Machito, and he remained its musical director until 1976. In 1943 his piece Tangá came about during a rehearsal. It began as a jam session on a repeated little piano figure, to which the bass, the saxophones and the trumpets added new layers one by one. Tangá is regarded as the first true Afro-Cuban jazz piece: jazz harmony, jazz soloists and an Afro-Cuban rhythm section in a single piece. In 1947 Bauzá introduced the conga player Chano Pozo to Gillespie, and out of that collaboration came Manteca.

Bauzá was the pivot between Cuba and the jazz of New York. Charlie Parker and Gillespie played with his orchestra, and he developed the concepts for the clave rhythm that musicians still use. After a quiet period he received renewed recognition around his eightieth year. He died in 1993.
artiest/mario-bauza.listen: Listen to Tangá by Machito and his Afro-Cubans and notice how the piece is built up: first a repeated little piano figure, then the bass, then the saxophones and the trumpets. Hear how the Afro-Cuban percussion runs on beneath while the jazz soloists improvise above.

artiest/marion-brown.text:
Marion Brown was an American alto saxophonist, composer, writer, visual artist and ethnomusicologist, born in Atlanta in 1931. He grew up with a single mother and was the grandson of an escaped slave from the Sea Islands of Georgia. Charlie Parker inspired him to learn the saxophone. He left school in the tenth grade, joined the army and was stationed, among other places, in Hokkaido. Later he studied music at Clark College and began law school at Howard University in Washington.

In 1962 he moved to New York. There he became friends with poets such as Amiri Baraka and with musicians such as Ornette Coleman and Archie Shepp. Coleman lent him his white plastic saxophone. Brown became a voice of the avant-garde jazz of the 1960s, played with John Coltrane, Archie Shepp and John Tchicai and can be heard on Coltrane's album Ascension from 1965. His own albums in the years that followed include Why Not in 1968, Porto Novo in 1969, Afternoon of a Georgia Faun in 1970 and Sweet Earth Flying in 1974. His music combines free jazz with memories of the American South and of African traditions.

The AllMusic reviewer Scott Yanow called him one of the clearest and most lyrical voices of the avant-garde of the 1960s. Brown died in 2010.
artiest/marion-brown.listen: Listen to Afternoon of a Georgia Faun and notice the lyrical alto saxophone and the small percussion instruments and bells that evoke the atmosphere of a Southern afternoon.

artiest/mariska-veres.text:
Mariska Veres was a Dutch singer, born in The Hague in 1947 as Maria Elisabeth Ender. Mariska is the Hungarian diminutive of Maria. Her father was the Hungarian violinist and bandleader Lajos Veres, of Roma descent, who had come to the Netherlands in 1939; her mother was born in Germany. At home she received piano and singing lessons, and she sang along with records by Helen Shapiro and Cliff Richard. At fifteen she became the singer of the Hague band Les Mystères, with which she won a talent contest in 1963. She then sang in a series of bands, including the Indo-rock group The Motowns, where she also played the organ.

In 1968 she was asked to join Shocking Blue, the band built around the guitarist and songwriter Robbie van Leeuwen, as a replacement for a singer who had to do military service. After Send Me a Postcard and Long and Lonesome Road came Venus in 1969, which became a worldwide hit and was the first Dutch record to reach number 1 in America. Shocking Blue then toured all over the world and had hits such as Never Marry a Railroad Man and Mighty Joe. In 1974 the group broke up. Veres then made solo singles, which were successful mainly in Germany, and later sang jazz with the Shocking Jazz Quintet. She died in 2006.

Veres stood out for her low, warm voice and her striking appearance, with black-rimmed eyes and long black hair, which was in fact a wig. She was one of the first Dutch female singers to become internationally known in rock music.
artiest/mariska-veres.listen: Listen to Venus by Shocking Blue and notice the guitar riff that opens the song. Hear how Mariska Veres then sings low and somewhat restrained, and how her voice grows more powerful in the chorus.

artiest/mariss-jansons.text:
Mariss Jansons was a Latvian conductor, born in 1943 in Riga. His mother Iraida was the diva of the Riga opera and his father Arvīds conducted the opera orchestra. His mother, who was Jewish, gave birth to him in a hiding place after being smuggled out of the Riga ghetto. He first learned the violin from his father. In 1956 he moved to Leningrad, where his father became assistant to Yevgeny Mravinsky and where he himself began to study conducting at the conservatory. In 1968 he caught the attention of Herbert von Karajan, but the Soviet authorities blocked his studies in Berlin. He then studied in Vienna with Hans Swarowsky and in Salzburg with Karajan.

His breakthrough came with the Oslo Philharmonic, where he was music director from 1979 to 2000. He later led the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra from 1997 to 2004, the Bavarian Radio Symphony Orchestra from 2003 to 2019 and the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra from 2004 to 2015. He made many recordings, including the symphonies of Tchaikovsky, such as the Sixth, the Pathétique, which was released in 1986. He was known for his performances of Mahler, Strauss and Russian composers such as Tchaikovsky, Rachmaninoff and Shostakovich. In a Bachtrack poll in 2015, critics ranked him the third-best conductor in the world.

Jansons died in 2019. He showed how a conductor can refine the sound of an orchestra and still stay close to the drama of the music.
artiest/mariss-jansons.listen: Listen to the beginning of Tchaikovsky's Sixth Symphony, the Pathétique, under Jansons and notice the dark, low sounds of the bassoon and the strings. Can you hear how the atmosphere slowly builds?

artiest/marius-constant.text:
Marius Constant was a French-Romanian composer and conductor, born in Bucharest in 1925. He studied piano and composition at the Bucharest conservatory and in 1944 received the George Enescu Prize. In 1946 he moved to Paris, where he studied with Olivier Messiaen, Arthur Honegger and Nadia Boulanger. In 1952 he won the Prix Italia with Le joueur de flûte, and from 1950 he became involved in the electronic music of Pierre Schaeffer's Groupe de Recherche de Musique Concrète.

From 1956 to 1966 he conducted for the Ballets de Paris of Roland Petit. During that time he wrote a great deal of ballet music for Petit and Maurice Béjart, such as Cyrano de Bergerac in 1959 and Éloge de la folie in 1966. His 24 Préludes pour Orchestre from 1958 were first performed under Leonard Bernstein and brought him fame. In the late 1950s he made short pieces for the music library of the American broadcaster CBS. For the second season of The Twilight Zone, a new signature tune was sought in 1960. The producer Lud Gluskin pasted two pieces by Constant together, Étrange No. 3 and Milieu No. 2, with repeating notes on electric guitar, bongos, brass and flutes. The result became Constant's best-known work.

He died in 2004. In the classical world he is known mainly for his ballet, but the guitar melody of The Twilight Zone has been heard by millions of viewers.
artiest/marius-constant.listen: Listen to the theme tune of The Twilight Zone and notice the repeated four notes on electric guitar and the bongos beneath. Can you hear how few notes are needed to create an atmosphere of unease?

artiest/mariya-takeuchi.text:
Mariya Takeuchi was born in 1955 in Taisha, now part of the city of Izumo in the Japanese prefecture of Shimane. She grew up in the family inn Takenoya and learned piano and guitar at an early age. The Beatles made an impression on her. In 1972 she lived for a year in Illinois as an exchange student, and she then studied English literature at Keio University. In 1978 she signed with RCA and released her debut album Beginning. Her first hits, such as September, brought her several newcomer-of-the-year awards in 1979.

In 1981 she broke her contract with RCA and took a break for a while. She married the singer and songwriter Tatsuro Yamashita. In 1984 she signed with Moon Records and Variety, her sixth album, was released and was commercially successful. Since 2001 each new album of hers has gone to number one on the Oricon charts. She also wrote songs for others. In Japan she is called the queen of city pop, and she has sold more than sixteen million records.

Her best-known song outside Japan is Plastic Love from Variety. When it came out, she did not think that Japanese-language music could travel the world. But in the mid-2010s the song spread through YouTube and through vaporwave and future funk, and it became the engine of a worldwide revival of city pop. City pop is smooth, urban Japanese pop music with funk, soul and disco.
artiest/mariya-takeuchi.listen: Listen to Plastic Love and notice the smooth, exciting bass line and the tight rhythm guitar. Can you hear how the vocals stay calm and elegant while the band keeps growing underneath?

artiest/mariza.text:
Mariza was born in 1973 as Marisa dos Reis Nunes in Lourenço Marques, in what was then Portuguese Mozambique. Her father was Portuguese, her mother Mozambican. When she was three, the family moved to Lisbon, where she grew up in the old districts of Mouraria and Alfama. From an early age she sang in many styles, including gospel, soul and jazz. Her father encouraged her to sing fado, because that tradition would give her more acceptance in the Portuguese community.

In 1999 Amália Rodrigues, the most famous fado singer, died. After that fado attracted new interest, and Mariza was asked to sing a tribute to her. That led in 2001 to her debut Fado em Mim, which sold a hundred thousand copies, in a genre where four thousand copies was already a success. Fado Curvo (2003) brought her international recognition and a BBC Radio 3 award for best European artist in world music. In 2004 she sang with Sting at the Olympic Games in Athens and won an EBBA Award. Transparente (2005) was recorded in Brazil and reached the top ten in the Netherlands, Spain and Finland, among other countries.

Mariza belongs to Nieuwe Fado. Her voice recalls the great divas of the genre, but her records reach a wider audience. She sang in halls such as Carnegie Hall and the Royal Albert Hall and became an ambassador of Portuguese culture.
artiest/mariza.listen: Listen to Ó Gente da Minha Terra and notice how her voice begins with great spaciousness and almost without accompaniment. What emotion do you hear in the long notes, and how does the Portuguese guitar fit in?

artiest/mark-fitz-gerald.text:
Mark Fitz-Gerald is a conductor who made recordings of film music from the early years of sound film. Nothing about his life was found in our sources. The Wikipedia page that came up for the name was about an episode of the television series Black Mirror and therefore does not belong to him. For that reason only what the album list shows is given here.

His recordings include Odna from 2008, the complete music for the film from 1929 to 1931, The Girlfriends and New Babylon, the world-premiere recording of the complete score, from 2011. Carmen also appeared in 2011. The titles Odna, The Girlfriends and New Babylon belong to films from the Soviet Union for which the composer Dmitri Shostakovich wrote the music, so these are recordings of lost or rarely played film music. The release of a complete score is important, because much film music of that era never appeared on record and could only be heard in the cinema.

The editors still have to establish who exactly Fitz-Gerald is, which orchestras and labels he works with and what his own background is.
artiest/mark-fitz-gerald.listen: Listen to an excerpt from New Babylon in Fitz-Gerald's recording and notice how the music accompanies the silent film: in short, sharp passages that change mood from scene to scene.

artiest/mark-knopfler.text:
Mark Knopfler is a British guitarist, singer, songwriter and producer. He was born in Glasgow in 1949, the son of a Hungarian-Jewish architect who had fled the Nazis in 1939, and grew up in Newcastle. As a teenager he wanted a red Stratocaster like Hank Marvin's, and he listened to Chet Atkins, Scotty Moore, B.B. King and Django Reinhardt. He worked as a journalist in Leeds, studied English and was a lecturer for three years. On an old acoustic guitar with a warped neck he discovered that he could only play with his fingers, without a plectrum. That is how he found his own sound.

In 1977 he started Dire Straits in London, with his brother David, the bassist John Illsley and the drummer Pick Withers. The debut album Dire Straits (1978) only took off when Sultans of Swing was reissued in early 1979. The Netherlands was one of the first countries where the band broke through. Communiqué (1979), Making Movies (1980), with Romeo and Juliet and Tunnel of Love, and Love Over Gold (1982) followed. Brothers in Arms (1985) became one of the best-selling albums ever. Knopfler also wrote film music, including for Local Hero (1983) and The Princess Bride (1987), and produced records for Bob Dylan and Tina Turner. After the end of Dire Straits in 1995 he continued as a solo artist.

Dire Straits began in the time of punk with short, stripped-down songs, but played narrative songs with long guitar solos in the tradition of blues and country. Knopfler's clear, flowing fingerstyle playing and his almost spoken singing made the band recognisable.
artiest/mark-knopfler.listen: Listen to Sultans of Swing by Dire Straits and notice the clear electric guitar that Knopfler plays with his fingers. Hear how he plays short runs between the lines and how the solo at the end grows ever faster and fuller.

artiest/mark-moore.text:
Mark Moore is a British DJ and producer from London, born in 1965. He began in 1983 as a DJ at The Mud Club and shortly afterwards got a regular night at the nightclub Heaven. Moore played electronic new wave by Yello, Cabaret Voltaire and Soft Cell, but he was also one of the first British DJs to play house from Chicago and techno from Detroit.

In 1988 he started S'Express, together with the co-producer Pascal Gabriel. The first single, Theme from S'Express, was released on the label Rhythm King and went to number one in England. The dance magazine Muzik later wrote that this song kick-started the British house scene. It was built from samples: pieces of other records, stuck together into a new dance track. Superfly Guy followed, which reached number five, and Hey Music Lover with the singer Billie Ray Martin. The album Original Soundtrack (1989) reached number 5 in England; the second album, Intercourse, appeared in 1991.

Moore kept making remixes, including for Erasure, Seal and Soft Cell, often together with William Orbit. From 2003 to 2007 he ran the club night Electrogogo in Soho, and in 2005 he started the label Umami Records. S'Express shows how acid house came about in England: a DJ who knew other people's records inside out took them apart in the studio and made something new of them.
artiest/mark-moore.listen: Listen in Theme from S'Express to how the song is built from separate fragments: a repeated disco bass line, short snatches of voice and little sounds that keep darting in between. Notice how little is actually played and how much is cut and pasted.

artiest/mark-ronson.text:
Mark Ronson is a British-American musician, producer, songwriter and DJ, born in 1975. He signed with Elektra Records and in 2003 released his debut album Here Comes the Fuzz, with guests from American hip hop. Sales were disappointing and he left the label, after which he founded his own label, Allido Records. In 2006 he became known for his production work for Lily Allen, Christina Aguilera and Amy Winehouse.

In 2007 he signed with Columbia Records and released Version, an album of covers in Motown-funk style. It featured Stop Me with Daniel Merriweather and Valerie with Amy Winehouse, both of which reached number two in the British chart. The album earned him a Brit Award. For Winehouse's album Back to Black he received a Grammy as producer of the year. His greatest international success was Uptown Funk from 2014, with Bruno Mars, the first single from Uptown Special from 2015. He dedicated that album to Winehouse. In 2018 he founded the label Zelig Records and, with Diplo, formed the duo Silk City, which won a Grammy with Electricity and Dua Lipa. He also won an Oscar for writing Shallow for the film A Star Is Born.

Ronson's sound brings old soul, funk and Motown back into modern pop, with live instruments and retro production technique. In doing so he gave singers such as Winehouse a contemporary classic sound.
artiest/mark-ronson.listen: Listen to Valerie by Amy Winehouse in Ronson's version and notice the lively brass and the tight drumming, which recalls Motown.

artiest/mark-snow.text:
Mark Snow was an American composer for film and television, born in 1946 in Brooklyn as Martin Fulterman. His grandfather came from Poland. He studied at the High School of Music and Art and at Juilliard, where with Michael Kamen he formed the band Emil and the Detectives, later the New York Rock and Roll Ensemble. An attempt to become a record producer failed. In 1974 he moved to Los Angeles, began composing and changed his name to Mark Snow.

His best-known work is the theme tune of the science fiction series The X-Files, for which he wrote the music from 1993 to 2001 and again from 2015 to 2018. He got the commission partly because he lived close to its creator Chris Carter. The theme cost him effort, because Carter rejected louder ideas. The melody took shape when Snow accidentally put his hand on the keyboard while an echo effect was switched on. The ethereal sound became the model for the rest. The theme was also released as a single, went to number one in France and reached number two in England. Snow also wrote the music for Smallville, Blue Bloods, Ghost Whisperer, Hart to Hart, Millennium, One Tree Hill, the new Twilight Zone from 2002 and Starsky and Hutch, and for two cinema films of The X-Files.

Snow showed how synthesizers and a simple motif can create tension. He died in 2025.
artiest/mark-snow.listen: Listen to the theme of The X-Files and notice the echo of the keyboard and the high, whistling melodic line. Can you hear how little it takes to create mystery?

artiest/markos-vamvakaris.text: Markos Vamvakaris fled the island of Syros at the age of twelve for the port of Piraeus, where he had all sorts of odd jobs and learned the bouzouki. In 1932 he made his first records, which he sang himself in a rough, sober voice. With Batis, Delias and Pagioumtzis he formed the famous Piraeus quartet. Songs such as Frangosyriani made the bouzouki the heart of rebetiko.
artiest/markos-vamvakaris.listen: Listen to Efumernam' ena vradi, one of his first recordings from 1932, and notice the bouzouki playing short, sharp runs between the lines.

artiest/marlena-shaw.text:
Marlena Shaw, born Marlina Burgess, was an American singer, born in 1939 in New Rochelle in the state of New York. Her uncle Jimmy Burgess, a jazz trumpeter, introduced her to good music: records by Dizzy Gillespie and Miles Davis, a lot of gospel and Al Hibbler, who knew how to phrase a song. In 1952 he took her to the Apollo Theater in Harlem to sing with his band. She began studying music at the teachers' college in Potsdam, but did not finish.

In the 1960s she sang in jazz clubs and in 1963 worked with the trumpeter Howard McGhee. She auditioned for John Hammond of Columbia, but was too nervous. Her breakthrough came in 1966 with a performance at the Playboy Club in Chicago, where she met people from Chess Records. Her first two albums appeared on the subsidiary label Cadet, including Out of Different Bags from 1968 and The Spice of Life from 1969. The song California Soul, written by Ashford and Simpson, later became a staple of the British rare groove scene and was heard in commercials. In 1972 she moved to the jazz label Blue Note. There Who Is This Bitch, Anyway? appeared in 1975. Her music has often been sampled in hip hop.

Shaw sang jazz, soul and funk with a powerful, playful voice and kept performing until her death in 2024.
artiest/marlena-shaw.listen: Listen to California Soul by Marlena Shaw and notice the tight rhythm section, the brass and the way her voice moves between soul and jazz. Can you hear why this song was later sampled so often?

artiest/marlene-dietrich.text:
Marlene Dietrich was born in Berlin in 1901. She studied the violin, but a wrist injury ended her dream of becoming a concert violinist. In the 1920s she appeared on stage as a revue girl and played small roles in theatre and in silent films. The breakthrough came with the role of the cabaret singer Lola Lola in Der blaue Engel (1930) by the director Josef von Sternberg. The film made her world famous and earned her a contract with Paramount Pictures in the United States. In Hollywood she appeared in, among others, Morocco, Shanghai Express and Blonde Venus.

In Der blaue Engel she sang Ich bin von Kopf bis Fuß auf Liebe eingestellt, the song that made her known as a singer. It became her trademark, together with Falling in Love Again, the English version. She recorded more songs in the 1930s. In the Second World War she performed for American troops, even just behind the front, and became known for Lili Marleen. From the 1950s she toured the world as a solo singer.

Her voice was low, her delivery restrained and almost spoken, full of irony. In this way she showed that a singer with a small voice can still captivate a large audience. Her style, her clothes and her bearing influenced many later artists.
artiest/marlene-dietrich.listen: Listen to Ich bin von Kopf bis Fuß auf Liebe eingestellt and notice her low, almost speaking voice. Can you hear how, with little volume and plenty of mockery, she gets a whole room in her power?

artiest/marshall-allen.text:
Marshall Allen is an American alto saxophonist from free and avant-garde jazz, born in 1924 in Louisville, Kentucky. He served in the Second World War in the 92nd Infantry Division, known as the Buffalo Soldiers, and was stationed in France. In Paris he studied the alto saxophone. In Europe he played with the pianist Art Simmons and the saxophonist James Moody. Besides the alto saxophone he plays flute, oboe, piccolo and the EWI, an electronic wind instrument.

His name is inextricably linked with Sun Ra, with whom he played almost exclusively from 1958 until Ra's death in 1993. Outside that, he recorded in 1964 with the group of Paul Bley and in the 1960s with the group of Olatunji. After Sun Ra's death, John Gilmore first led the Arkestra, after which Allen took over the leadership in 1995. Allen is known for explosive, abrasive sound effects on the alto saxophone, a style that is also described as pyrotechnic. He said he wanted to play on a broader sound basis than just chords. Scott Yanow called his playing Johnny Hodges from another dimension. Later albums under his own name include Ceremonial Healing from 2019, Flow States from 2020 and Dancing Shadows from 2022. In 2004 he celebrated his eightieth birthday on stage with the Arkestra.

Allen keeps the cosmic legacy of Sun Ra alive. He shows that free jazz can have a collective, theatrical and almost festive character.
artiest/marshall-allen.listen: Listen to the Sun Ra Arkestra under Allen and notice the abrasive outbursts of the alto saxophone above the rhythm of the group. Can you hear how chaos and ensemble playing alternate?

artiest/marshall-jefferson.text:
Marshall Jefferson was born in 1959 in Chicago and is often called the father of house music. He was the son of a police officer and a teacher, studied accountancy for a while and worked at a post office. As a teenager he loved hard rock. At the beginning of the 1980s, through friends, he became involved in the emerging house scene of Chicago. At first he disliked dance music, until he heard the DJ Ron Hardy play. After that he wanted to make records himself.

In 1985 his first production came out, the EP Go Wild Rhythm Trax, under the name Virgo. A year later Move Your Body (The House Music Anthem) appeared on Trax Records, the first house track with piano. The record became a big hit in Chicago and in England introduced many listeners to the new genre. In the 1980s Jefferson recorded under several names, such as Virgo, Jungle Wonz, Truth and On the House, and produced for CeCe Rogers, Sterling Void and the first two albums of Ten City. In March 1987 he was in England with Frankie Knuckles for the first house tour.

His style is deep and melodic, with heavy piano riffs and grand-sounding strings. In this way he helped lay the foundation of deep house. Move Your Body was later used in the film 24 Hour Party People and in the game Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, and received a remix with Solardo in 2019.
artiest/marshall-jefferson.listen: Listen to Move Your Body (The House Music Anthem) and notice the piano chords that keep returning. Can you hear how the bouncing rhythm and the piano together get a party going?

artiest/martha-argerich.text:
Martha Argerich is an Argentine concert pianist, born in 1941 in Buenos Aires. She began playing the piano at the age of three and at five received lessons from Vincenzo Scaramuzza, who stressed lyricism and feeling. At eight she gave her first concert. Six years later her family moved to Europe, where she studied with Friedrich Gulda in Austria and later with Stefan Askenase and Maria Curcio. In 1957, at sixteen, she won both the Busoni Competition and the Geneva International Music Competition. A personal and artistic crisis followed.

Her international career began after her victory at the International Chopin Piano Competition of 1965. She made records such as Début Recital from 1961 and the recording of Prokofiev's Third Piano Concerto and Ravel's Piano Concerto in G from 1967. She is known for her interpretations of Chopin, Ravel, Liszt, Prokofiev and Schumann. Since the 1980s she has chosen mainly ensemble playing, with musicians such as Nelson Freire, Mischa Maisky and Gidon Kremer.

Argerich is regarded as one of the greatest pianists of our time. She combines a blazing technique with an impulsive, almost improvised expression, and shows how classical music can sound direct and exciting.
artiest/martha-argerich.listen: Listen to Ravel's Piano Concerto in G in her recording and notice the fast, jazzy opening and the very calm, singing middle section. Can you hear how she creates the difference in mood?

artiest/martha-reeves-en-the-vandellas.text:
Martha and the Vandellas, from 1967 to 1973 Martha Reeves & the Vandellas, was an American girl group from Detroit that began in 1957. The friends Annette Beard, Rosalind Ashford and Gloria Williams first sang as the Del-Phis on local stages, in churches and at schools. Martha Reeves joined and became lead singer in 1962, when Williams left. In 1960 Reeves had already had a first recording contract with Checker Records, but those records disappeared without trace. She then auditioned at Motown, where the group signed to the subsidiary label Gordy Records.

The hits came quickly: Heat Wave in 1963, Quicksand in 1963, Dancing in the Street in 1964, Nowhere to Run in 1965, I'm Ready for Love in 1966, Jimmy Mack and Honey Chile in 1967. Six songs reached the American top ten and thirteen the top twenty of the R&B chart, with two reaching number one. Albums include Come and Get These Memories and Heat Wave from 1963 and Dance Party from 1965. Reeves's voice, powerful and full of gospel, was out in front. The recordings came from the Hitsville USA studio, with the close-knit bond of the Motown musicians.

In 1995 members of the group were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Their hits remain cornerstones of the Motown sound.
artiest/martha-reeves-en-the-vandellas.listen: Listen to Dancing in the Street and notice the driving drums, the horn-like brass and the fiery voice of Martha Reeves. Can you hear how the chorus sounds like an invitation?

artiest/martial-solal.text:
Martial Solal was a French jazz pianist and composer, born in 1927 in Algiers to Algerian-Jewish parents. His mother, an opera singer, made sure he learned clarinet, saxophone and piano. In 1942 he was expelled from school because of his parents' Jewish origins, when the Vichy regime followed German policy. He learned a great deal by playing along to music from the radio and at fifteen was already performing for American soldiers.

In 1950 he settled in Paris, where he played with Django Reinhardt and with American expatriates such as Sidney Bechet and Don Byas. In the late 1950s he led a quartet and sometimes a big band. He wrote more than twenty film scores, including for Breathless by Jean-Luc Godard from 1960. In 1963 he played at the Newport Jazz Festival, with the bassist Guy Pedersen and the drummer Daniel Humair. From 1968 he played in Europe and the United States with Lee Konitz. Albums include En Liberté from 1965, Electrodes from 1966 and Action from 1969.

Jean-Pierre Thiollet called his playing brilliant, unique and intellectual. Solal said that you must make people believe that something is very easy, even if it is very difficult. He died in 2024, ninety-seven years old, and was an example of a European pianist who sought his own paths in jazz.
artiest/martial-solal.listen: Listen to a recording by Solal and notice how he takes a familiar theme apart and sends it off in unexpected directions, while the playing still sounds easy.

artiest/martin-frost.text:
Martin Fröst is a Swedish clarinettist and conductor, born in 1970 in Uppsala. He began on the violin at five and on the clarinet at nine, after hearing a recording of Jack Brymer playing Mozart's clarinet concerto. He studied in Stockholm with Sölve Kingstedt and Kjell-Inge Stevensson and in Hanover with Hans Deinzer. At seventeen he played his first concert with the orchestra of the Royal Swedish Academy of Music.

As a soloist he has played with the great orchestras of the world, such as the New York Philharmonic, the Concertgebouw Orchestra, the London Symphony Orchestra and the Wiener Symphoniker. He is the first clarinettist to receive the Léonie Sonning Music Prize, an award also received by Stravinsky, Bernstein and Miles Davis. In the 2022-23 season he was the only wind player to be artist in residence at the Concertgebouw Orchestra. In 2019 he became chief conductor of the Swedish Chamber Orchestra. Composers such as John Adams, Krzysztof Penderecki, Anna Clyne and Anders Hillborg have written works especially for him. His first albums include The Pied Piper of the Opera from 1993 and French Beauties and Swedish Beasts from 1994. Fröst also makes multimedia projects with music, choreography and lighting design, in which he plays the clarinet, conducts and presents.

He shows how a classical soloist can break through the boundaries between music, dance and theatre.
artiest/martin-frost.listen: Listen to Fröst in Mozart's clarinet concerto and notice the soft, singing tone in the slow movement. Can you hear how the clarinet sounds almost like a human voice?

artiest/martin-galway.text:
Martin Galway was born in 1966 in Belfast and grew into one of the best-known composers of chiptune, the music of the early home computers. He later moved to Manchester and in the 1980s wrote music as a freelancer for games on the Commodore 64 and the ZX Spectrum, including for the publisher Ocean Software. His work for Comic Bakery, Rambo: First Blood Part II, Green Beret, Parallax and Wizball was heard by thousands of players every time they loaded a game.

Galway got a great deal out of the SID sound chip of the Commodore 64, a three-voice chip that was really intended for simple synthesizer sounds. With it he made melodies that sounded like a small ensemble, with their own walking bass, fast arpeggios and rhythms. He was the first to publish samples on that computer: the music you heard while Arkanoid was loading contained drum sounds that he had improvised himself by playing with the volume register.

In 1990 he became audio director at Origin Systems, where he worked on games such as Wing Commander and Strike Commander. Later he worked as audio director for other studios, including Digital Anvil and Cloud Imperium Games. His music lives on in remixes, covers and concerts of the retro gaming community, and in 2024 he made his original C64 source files public. For pop history he is important because he showed that a computer game can have a musical language of its own.
artiest/martin-galway.listen: Listen to the title music of Comic Bakery or Wizball and notice how three voices sound like a complete ensemble: who plays the bass line, who the melody, and where do you hear a rhythm?

artiest/martin-garrix.text:
Martin Garrix's real name is Martijn Garritsen, and he was born in 1996 in Amstelveen. At eight he learned to play the guitar. That same year he saw the Dutch DJ Tiësto perform at the opening of the Olympic Games in Athens. It made such an impression that he downloaded the music program FL Studio and began making tracks himself. Later he followed the production course at the Herman Brood Academie in Utrecht.

After a remix for Enrique Iglesias, he signed in 2012 with the Dutch dance label Spinnin' Records. On 16 June 2013 Animals was released, an instrumental track with a hard, buzzing synthesizer melody that bursts loose after a long build-up. The song became a hit in a large number of countries. Garrix became the youngest artist to reach number 1 on Beatport, the big online store for dance music, and in November 2013 Animals reached number 1 in the British chart. He was seventeen at the time. In 2014 he was the youngest DJ ever to headline the Ultra Music Festival in Miami.

After that Garrix grew into one of the biggest DJs in the world. He made hits such as In the Name of Love and Scared to Be Lonely, founded his own label Stmpd Rcrds in 2016 and was named number 1 on DJ Mag's list of best DJs several times. His story shows how electronic music comes into being in the twenty-first century: with software on a laptop, made by a teenager who saw his role models on television.
artiest/martin-garrix.listen: Listen to Animals and follow the build-up: the tension rises, the rhythm speeds up, and then everything briefly falls silent. Notice what happens next, as the heavy synthesizer melody bursts loose in the drop.

artiest/martin-hannett.text:
Martin Hannett was a producer from Manchester who helped shape the sound of British post-punk. He was born in 1948, studied chemistry and played bass guitar in local bands. In 1977, under the name Martin Zero, he produced the EP Spiral Scratch by Buzzcocks, one of the first punk records to appear outside the major record companies. He then worked with the poet John Cooper Clarke and became one of the founders and directors of Factory Records, Tony Wilson's label.

At Factory he produced everything Joy Division recorded in the studio, including the albums Unknown Pleasures (1979) and Closer (1980) and the single Love Will Tear Us Apart (1980), which only became a hit after the death of the singer Ian Curtis. Hannett treated the studio as an instrument, like the German producer Conny Plank. He worked with echoes, delays, filters and loops, and mixed the drums with synthesizer sounds. As a result the drums on Unknown Pleasures sound dry and almost mechanical, with a lot of empty space around them. He also worked with New Order, The Durutti Column, A Certain Ratio, Magazine, U2 and later Happy Mondays.

After leaving Factory his career fell into decline through alcohol and heroin. He died in 1991 in Manchester of heart failure, aged 42. His gravestone says that he created The Manchester Sound. In the films 24 Hour Party People (2002) and Control (2007) he appears as a character.
artiest/martin-hannett.listen: Listen in She's Lost Control to the drums: short, tight and dry, almost like a drum machine. Notice too how the bass carries the melody and how Ian Curtis's vocals seem to stand in a bare, cold space.

artiest/martin-hayes.text:
Martin Hayes is an Irish fiddler from County Clare, born in 1962 into a family full of musicians. His father P.J. Hayes played the fiddle and for years led the Tulla Céilí Band, which had been founded in 1946, partly by his uncle Paddy Canny. Martin began at the age of seven, was taught by his father and at thirteen won an All-Ireland Fiddle Competition for the first time. In 1981 and 1982 he became senior champion. As a teenager he played for seven years in the Tulla Céilí Band.

In 1985 he moved to Chicago, where he played in the Irish sessions and in bars played all kinds of music to make ends meet. In 1989 he formed the group Midnight Court with the guitarist Dennis Cahill, which combined traditional Irish music with rock. His solo career began in 1993 with the album Martin Hayes, followed by Under the Moon in 1995. From 1996 he formed an acoustic duo with Cahill. Their album The Lonesome Touch appeared in 1997, Welcome Here Again in 2008.

Hayes plays calmly and lyrically, with a lot of space between the notes. A reviewer in the New York Times compared the duo's approach with the quartets of Steve Reich and with Sketches of Spain by Miles Davis. Together with Cahill, Iarla Ó Lionáird, Caoimhín Ó Raghallaigh and Doveman he formed The Gloaming, whose first album won the Meteor Choice Music Prize in 2014. Since 2003 he has run the Masters of Tradition festival in Bantry. In this way he kept the Irish tradition alive and brought it to an audience beyond the session pub.
artiest/martin-hayes.listen: Listen to a reel or jig from The Lonesome Touch and notice the slowness: how does Hayes leave space between the notes, and what does Cahill's guitar do in that silence?

artiest/martin-o-donnell.text:
Martin O'Donnell is an American composer and sound designer, born in 1955. He received piano lessons from his mother, dreamed as a schoolboy of a rock band and studied composition at the Wheaton College Conservatory of Music and the University of Southern California. In Chicago he first worked in film and television. Together with Michael Salvatori he founded the production company TotalAudio, which made jingles for fifteen years, including for Mr. Clean and Flintstones Chewable Vitamins.

When his company did the sound for the game Riven in 1997, he moved into game music. For Bungie he wrote the music for Myth: The Fallen Lords and Myth II: Soulblighter, then for Oni. In 1999 he joined Bungie, ten days before Microsoft bought the company. His best-known work is the music of Halo, starting with Halo: Original Soundtrack in 2002, followed by Halo 2, Halo 3, Halo 3: ODST and Halo Reach. The theme opens with Gregorian chant and a classical orchestra, to get the old-fashioned and grand feeling that the design team wanted. For ODST he chose a jazz-like sound, fitting the atmosphere of a film noir.

In 2014 he wrote the music for Destiny and left Bungie. He then founded the studio Highwire Games, for which he made the music for Golem. He showed that a game soundtrack can also stand up on CD or in the concert hall. In 2015 Halo was voted into the Classic FM Hall of Fame by listeners for the first time.
artiest/martin-o-donnell.listen: Listen to the theme of Halo: Original Soundtrack and notice the opening with choral singing, after which orchestra and rhythm join in. Can you hear how the music wants to sound both ancient and grand at once?

artiest/martin-o-donnell-en-michael-salv.text: Martin O'Donnell and Michael Salvatori first wrote advertising music together in Chicago. For the game studio Bungie they made the music for Myth (1997). Halo: Combat Evolved (2001) followed. The Halo theme begins with a men's choir in the style of Gregorian chant, after which strings and percussion come in; elsewhere in the score electric guitars can also be heard. This mixture of old and new gave the science fiction world a solemn, mysterious character. The music in the game responded to what the player did and became more tense during fights. The theme returned in Halo 2 and Halo 3 (2007). For Destiny (2014) they worked with Paul McCartney. Halo brought game music closer to the film score.
artiest/martin-o-donnell-en-michael-salv.listen: Listen to the men's choir in church style and how strings and drums then drive up the tempo.

artiest/martin-rushent.text:
Martin Rushent was born in 1948 in Enfield near London and became one of the most important British producers of punk and new wave. He began in the early 1970s as a sound engineer at Advision Studios, where he rose to chief engineer and then went freelance. At United Artists he recorded sessions with, among others, Shirley Bassey and Buzzcocks, and he persuaded the label to sign the Stranglers, on condition that he would produce their music. He made their albums Rattus Norvegicus, No More Heroes and Black and White.

Around 1980 he wanted to get away from guitar bands and learned to work with a Linn LM-1 drum machine, a Roland MC-8 Microcomposer and a Jupiter-8 synthesizer. He built his own studio Genetic, with a Synclavier and a Fairlight CMI. There he recorded Homosapien, Pete Shelley's first solo album. Those recordings attracted the attention of Virgin, which asked him to produce the Human League. The album Dare from 1981 earned him a BRIT Award in 1982 as best British producer. Generation X, Altered Images and the Go-Go's also worked with him in the 1980s.

In the 1990s he distanced himself from the studio and opened a dance club at Greenham Common. Later he built a home studio and produced, among others, the Pipettes and Does It Offend You, Yeah?, whose singer is his son James. Rushent died in 2011. His work shows how punk producers began to use machines and so pointed the way to synth-pop.
artiest/martin-rushent.listen: Listen to a track from Dare by the Human League and notice how synthesizers and drum machine carry the rhythm: where can you still hear the raw energy of punk, and where already the smooth voice of electronics?

artiest/marty-robbins.text:
Marty Robbins was born in 1925 as Martin David Robinson in Glendale, Arizona. At seventeen he joined the American navy and served in the Solomon Islands. There he learned to play the guitar, began writing songs and fell in love with Hawaiian music. After the war he played in clubs around Phoenix and got his own radio show and later the television show Western Caravan. Little Jimmy Dickens helped him get a recording contract.

In 1952 he had his first number one on the country chart with I'll Go On Alone, followed in 1956 by Singing the Blues. His best-known record is the album Gunfighter Ballads and Trail Songs from 1959, featuring El Paso. The follow-up More Gunfighter Ballads and Trail Songs came in 1960, and The Return of the Gunfighter in 1963. He also wrote Big Iron, a song that goes back to the stories of his grandfather, who is said to have been a Texas Ranger. Robbins recorded more than five hundred songs and sixty albums and was a fixture at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville.

His voice was soft and clear, and he could sing a western ballad as convincingly as a rock 'n' roll number or a Hawaiian song. An album such as Song of the Islands from 1957 shows that range. He was also a keen stock car driver in NASCAR. He received two Grammy Awards and was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame and the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame. His western stories remained the example for country singers who wanted to tell a whole drama in a few minutes.
artiest/marty-robbins.listen: Listen to El Paso and follow the story: who is telling it, what happens, and how do the guitar and the soft accompaniment support the tension?

artiest/marvin-gaye.text:
Marvin Gaye was born on 2 April 1939 in Washington, D.C., the son of a preacher. He sang in church as early as the age of four, where his father accompanied him on the piano. His career began with Harvey Fuqua, who took him into his group The Moonglows. In the early 1960s he went solo and signed with Tamla, a Motown label.

At Motown he scored hits such as How Sweet It Is (to Be Loved by You), Ain't That Peculiar and I Heard It Through the Grapevine. He also sang duets, above all with Tammi Terrell, with whom he recorded Ain't No Mountain High Enough, and with Diana Ross. In 1971 What's Going On was released, an album over which he had largely taken control himself. In doing so he was one of the first Motown artists to break free from the label's fixed production machine. Let's Get It On, I Want You and Here, My Dear followed. In 1982 he moved to Columbia and had his greatest success with Sexual Healing.

Gaye helped define the sound of Motown and soul in the 1960s and 1970s. His voice could be soft and pleading, and with overdubs he sang his own harmonies. His work from the 1970s later influenced movements such as quiet storm and neo-soul. On 1 April 1984, a day before his 45th birthday, he was shot dead by his own father.
artiest/marvin-gaye.listen: Listen to I Heard It Through the Grapevine. Notice the menacing atmosphere of the accompaniment and how tormented Gaye sounds as he sings about the rumour that his lover wants to leave him.

artiest/marvin-hamlisch.text: Marvin Hamlisch was born in 1944 in Manhattan. As early as 1951 he was admitted to the pre-college division of the Juilliard School. Later he studied at Queens College. At the Academy Awards ceremony of 1974 he won three Oscars. Two were for The Way We Were (1973): for the score and for the title song. The third was for The Sting (1973), for which he adapted ragtimes by Scott Joplin, such as The Entertainer. For the Bond film The Spy Who Loved Me (1977) he co-wrote the song Nobody Does It Better. Sophie's Choice (1982) followed later. On Broadway he wrote A Chorus Line (1975), which received a Tony and a Pulitzer Prize. He won an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar and a Tony. He died in 2012.
artiest/marvin-hamlisch.listen: In The Sting, listen to the ragtime piano with its walking left hand and shifted accents in the melody, and compare that with the disco rhythms in the Bond music.
